name: Elena Zhang

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I cycle in to the firm for about nine, and I work in the employment team, acting for workers rather than bosses. My clients are warehouse staff, care workers, a lot of people dismissed unfairly or treated badly because of their race or a pregnancy. I spend the day reading email chains, drafting witness statements and preparing for the employment tribunal, which is the court that hears work disputes. On Wednesdays I'm usually in a hearing.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like it when someone who's been ignored for months finally gets an apology and a payout. What wears me out is the volume, and the pay. I earn less than my friends from law school who went to bigger firms, and I've got a credit card from moving flats that never quite goes down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, now can we talk about the real problems at work, like zero-hours contracts. Online I'd share something dry about all the money spent on hype. At work I'd just shrug and get on with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it barely changes anything. I already use AI now and then to summarise long email chains, and I'd keep doing that. My worry is the one I have now: I'm paid less than friends from law school, and my savings wouldn't cover one month if the firm had a bad year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my caseload and keep using the summary tool where it's proven to save time. I'd try to put a hundred a month aside, starting in January. And I'd push the firm again on recognising a union for the support staff, which has been stuck for a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly steady. A bit annoyed that the hype ate so much attention, and still tight about money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill goes unpaid first if a month goes wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The credit card from when we moved flats. I already pay only the minimum on it. Rent and my partner's train pass come first, always.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at your firm would welcome a plateau most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our senior partner, honestly. He spent last spring worried about clients asking why they should pay for hours a computer could do. A plateau would let him stop worrying and keep billing the old way.

say: I'd say the real problems at work are things like **zero-hours contracts**.
Online I'd post something dry about the **money spent on hype**.
think: AI barely changes my day; I'd keep using it to **summarise emails**.
I'm paid less than law school friends and **couldn't cover a month** if the firm struggled.
do: Keep my caseload and the **summary tool** where it proves useful.
Put **a hundred a month** aside from January.
Press the firm again to **recognise a union** for support staff.
feel: Fairly **steady**, annoyed at the hype and still **tight about money**.
S0.quote: I'm paid less than friends from law school, and my savings wouldn't cover one month if the firm had a bad year.
fieldNote: Her worry is **money**, and it predates any talk of AI.
She already uses AI in a **measured** way and would carry on.
Her instinct is **collective**: she brings up the support staff union unprompted.

steps.text: Use the email summary tool only on long disclosure bundles
Put a hundred a month aside from January
Press the firm to recognise a union for support staff

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say firms are going to use this to cut juniors and paralegals and call it efficiency. I'd want rules on how employers can use AI to replace staff, and I'd say that at work and online. Employment law is my job, so people would expect me to have a view.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think my firm hires fewer people like me. First drafts, witness statement outlines, checking documents for disclosure, that's most of my week. I'd survive if I get good at checking the machine, but my pay probably stays flat for years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the firm's AI training properly this time, not half-listen, in the first three months. I'd ask to take more tribunal hearings, because standing up in front of a judge is harder to hand to software. And I'd cut the Saturday takeaways and the streaming services to get a month saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, with a bit of anger mixed in. Like the ground's moving and everyone's pretending it's fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said your pay stays flat. What does that mean at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means my partner and I stay renting. We'd been talking about saving for a deposit in five years, and that slides to never. He's a teacher, so his pay won't rescue us either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You want rules on replacing staff, but you'd also learn the tools. Is that a contradiction?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really, I think. I can want the bus to have brakes and still need to ride it. If I refuse the AI tools, I'm just the first lawyer the firm lets go.

say: I'd say firms will **cut juniors** and paralegals and call it efficiency.
I'd call for **rules** on employers using AI to replace staff.
think: Drafting and **disclosure checks** are most of my week, so my firm hires fewer like me.
I'd survive by checking the machine, but my **pay stays flat**.
do: Do the firm's **AI training** properly within three months.
Ask for more **tribunal hearings**, which are harder to hand to software.
Cut takeaways and **streaming** to save a month.
feel: **Anxious** with some **anger**, as if everyone pretends the ground isn't moving.
S1.quote: If I refuse the AI tools, I'm just the first lawyer the firm lets go.
fieldNote: She holds two positions at once: **regulate it** and **learn it**.
A house **deposit** slides from five years to never in this picture.
She sees **courtroom work** as the part of her job that lasts.

steps.text: Complete the firm's AI drafting training within three months
Cancel streaming services and Saturday takeaways
Write to her MP about rules on replacing staff with AI

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the biggest employment law question of my lifetime and nobody's ready. I'd campaign for a pause on mass redundancies and for some sort of income support. I'd probably post more in a month than I have in five years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years means my job, as it is now, is mostly gone by 2028. My work is reading, writing and arguing, all thinking work, so the robots coming in 2031 don't buy me anything. Being the human who stands up in the tribunal might last, but there won't be enough of that to go round.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to the partners in the first month and ask straight out what the plan is. I'd pick up every redundancy case I could, because there'd be a flood of them in the first year. And I'd look at whether my partner and I could move somewhere cheaper, maybe nearer his parents.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. Like the floor's going and I've only got a month's rent on the table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My parents run a small shop and paid for a lot of law school. I'd tell my parents I'm fine before I believed it myself. That's the bit I hate thinking about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said there'd be a flood of redundancy cases. Is that work for you or a warning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both. For a year or so, lots of people would need someone to fight their dismissal. Then the AI would be doing those claims too, and I'd be one of the people filing one.

say: I'd call it the **biggest employment question** of my lifetime.
I'd campaign for a **pause on mass redundancies** and income support.
think: My work is all thinking, so my job is **mostly gone** by 2028.
The **robot delay** to 2031 buys me nothing; tribunal advocacy alone won't go round.
do: Ask the partners for their **staffing plan** in the first month.
Take every **redundancy case** that comes in during the first year.
Look at **moving** nearer my partner's parents for cheaper rent.
feel: **Frightened**, with only a **month's rent** to stand on.
S2.quote: I'd tell my parents I'm fine before I believed it myself.
fieldNote: She sees a brief **boom in redundancy work**, then her own claim.
**Guilt** toward her parents, who funded law school, runs under everything.
Her answer is part campaign, part **retreat** to cheaper housing.

steps.text: Campaign for a pause on mass redundancies and income support
Take on every redundancy claim in the first year
Look at moving nearer her partner's parents for cheaper rent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years, so let's write the rules now. Unions, firms and government should agree how redundancies and retraining work before 2031. I'd say it calmly, because panic doesn't help anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is enough to make one real move, if I start early. I'd be 32, probably still renting, and I'd want to be in a role where a person has to be accountable, like a union legal officer. The writing and checking part of my job is gone either way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In year one I'd apply to the union's legal department, because they'll need people who know employment law when the redundancies start. I'd use AI tools at work every day to stay useful in the meantime. And I'd save by staying in our small flat instead of moving to the bigger one we'd looked at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but I could sleep. It feels like a plan instead of a fall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you give up to stay in the small flat?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A spare room for my partner's marking, mostly. He'd do his marking at the kitchen table, which he hates. We'd keep the extra hundred and fifty a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a person has to be accountable. Would that still be true in 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I honestly don't know. I think people will want a human name on a decision that costs them their job, at least for a while. I'd bet on that, but I wouldn't bet the rent on it.

say: I'd say we have **five years**, so write the rules now.
I'd want unions, firms and government to agree **redundancy and retraining** before 2031.
think: Five years is enough for **one real move** if I start early.
I'd want a role where a person stays **accountable**, like a union legal officer.
do: Apply to the **union's legal department** in year one.
Use **AI tools daily** at the firm to stay useful.
Stay in the **small flat** and keep the extra money.
feel: **Worried** but able to sleep; it feels like **a plan**.
S3.quote: People will want a human name on a decision that costs them their job, at least for a while.
fieldNote: Five years moves her from fear to a **concrete exit**.
Her bet on **human accountability** is honest about its limits.
Small sacrifices at home, like the **spare room**, carry the plan.

steps.text: Apply to the union's legal department in the first year
Use AI drafting tools daily at the firm
Stay in the small flat and save the extra rent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a real chance to do this fairly, if we start now. I'd push for proper retraining funds and rules on AI in hiring. I'd say it at every conference I could afford to go to, which isn't many.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years feels almost manageable. My job would change a lot before 2036, but I'd be 37 with time to move into something with real responsibility. The worry is that ten years makes everyone lazy, me included.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for a part-time mediation course in the next two years, so I can settle workplace disputes instead of only drafting claims. I'd start using AI properly at work once the firm picks a tool. And I'd keep the savings habit going, aiming for three months by 2028.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a way I can live with. More like a long to-do list than a threat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who pays for the mediation course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the firm first, because it's useful to them too. If they say no, it's about eight hundred, and I'd spread it over a year. My partner says I should do it anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said ten years makes everyone lazy. Would it make you lazy?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, yes, if I'm honest. I'm good at deciding to do things next year. A ten-year warning is the kind of deadline I'd leave until year eight.

say: I'd call ten years a **real chance** to do this fairly.
I'd push for **retraining funds** and rules on AI in hiring.
think: My job changes, but at 37 I'd have **time to move**.
Ten years risks making everyone **lazy**, me included.
do: Start a part-time **mediation course** within two years.
Use the firm's **AI tool** properly once it's chosen.
feel: **Uneasy** but livable, like a **long to-do list**.
S4.quote: A ten-year warning is the kind of deadline I'd leave until year eight.
fieldNote: With a decade, her own job feels **safe for now**, even as it changes.
She's frank about **procrastination** as her real risk.
**Mediation** is her chosen route out of pure drafting work.

steps.text: Enrol in a part-time mediation course within two years
Start using the firm's chosen AI tool every day
Build three months of savings by 2028
Push for retraining funds and AI hiring rules at conferences

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd have no time and no money to change course. What would help is a law that makes firms consult and give proper notice before replacing people with AI, and funded retraining I could do while still working.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe that it's odd to be an employment lawyer in this. I spend my days helping people who lost their jobs unfairly, and I can see a future where I'm the one in the waiting room.

headlineQuote: I spend my days helping people who lost their jobs unfairly, and I can see a future where I'm the one in the waiting room.
portrait: Elena is a **27-year-old** employment lawyer for workers at a mid-size firm, paid less than her law school friends.
She rents with her partner, a **teacher**, with **under a month** saved and a credit card balance.
She uses AI **now and then** and would use more once her firm settles on a tool.
Her mood climbs to **alarmed** as the warning shrinks, since her work is almost all thinking.
She meets each picture with **rules and a plan**: tribunal work, union jobs, mediation.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because she'd have no time or **money** to change course.
whatWouldHelp: A law making firms **consult** and give proper notice before replacing staff with AI.
**Funded retraining** she could do while still working.
